req1: Send her to CT pulmonary angiogram right away
She is shocked. A bedside echocardiogram can show right ventricular strain without moving an unstable patient.
Check a D-dimer and wait for the result
D-dimer cannot rule in PE and wastes time in a shocked patient. Use bedside echo.
req2: Give 2 litres of crystalloid rapidly
A failing right ventricle dilates further with large fluid volumes. Use a small bolus and early noradrenaline.
Give a GTN infusion to reduce afterload
Nitrates drop preload and worsen hypotension in massive PE.
req3: Wait for the CT before anticoagulating
With a high probability of massive PE and no contraindication, anticoagulate immediately.
Start warfarin tonight
Warfarin takes days to work and is prothrombotic at first. Use IV unfractionated heparin.
req4: Continue heparin alone and observe
Persistent shock in massive PE is an indication for systemic thrombolysis.
Insert an IVC filter as the main treatment
Filters do not treat the existing clot or the shock. Thrombolysis restores perfusion.
req5: Discharge on 2 weeks of enoxaparin
Provoked PE still needs at least 3 months of anticoagulation, and she needs ICU monitoring after thrombolysis.
Stop anticoagulation once she stabilises
Stopping early risks recurrence. Plan long-term anticoagulation.

req1: Give aspirin 300 mg for presumed ACS
Tearing pain radiating to the back suggests dissection. Check bilateral blood pressures and pulses before antiplatelets.
Send him straight to the cath lab
Coronary angiography in dissection delays surgery and can be fatal. Confirm the diagnosis first.
req2: Start heparin for ACS
Anticoagulation in aortic dissection increases bleeding and death. Withhold it.
Thrombolyse for the ST changes
Thrombolysis in dissection is often fatal. ST changes can reflect coronary ostial involvement.
req3: Hydralazine alone to lower the pressure
A vasodilator alone causes reflex tachycardia, increasing shear stress. Beta blockade comes first.
No analgesia so that pain can be monitored
Pain drives catecholamines and blood pressure. Treat it aggressively.
req4: Medical management only for a type A dissection
Type A dissection is a surgical emergency with high mortality without surgery.
Wait for the dual antiplatelet effect to wear off before surgery
Delay increases mortality. Operate now and correct coagulation.
req5: Discharge with blood pressure target of 160 systolic
Strict control below 120 systolic reduces progression of the residual dissection.
No follow-up imaging needed after repair
The residual descending dissection needs serial imaging.

req1: Lay him flat and give sedation for agitation
Lying flat with sedation risks aspiration of blood. Sit upright and consider early intubation.
Insert a nasogastric tube to lavage blood
Lavage does not help and risks variceal trauma. Protect the airway.
req2: Transfuse to a haemoglobin of 12 g/dL
Liberal transfusion raises portal pressure and increases rebleeding and mortality. Target 7 to 8 g/dL.
Give 4 litres of saline to restore the pressure
Large crystalloid volumes raise portal pressure and worsen bleeding. Transfuse restrictively.
req3: Propranolol IV for the varices
Beta blockers are for secondary prevention, not acute bleeding. They worsen hypotension. Use terlipressin or octreotide.
Skip antibiotics, there is no sign of infection
Prophylactic antibiotics reduce infection, rebleeding and death in cirrhotic GI bleeding.
req4: Endoscopy electively in 48 hours
Variceal bleeding needs endoscopy within 12 hours.
Sengstaken tube as first-line definitive treatment
Balloon tamponade is a temporary bridge if endoscopy fails, not definitive therapy.
req5: Sedate him with benzodiazepines for the confusion
Benzodiazepines worsen hepatic encephalopathy. Use lactulose.
No ascitic tap needed if he has no abdominal pain
SBP is often silent. A diagnostic tap is recommended in every cirrhotic admission.

req1: Wait for a CT to confirm necrotising fasciitis
Imaging delays surgery. Pain out of proportion with systemic toxicity needs an immediate surgical consult.
Treat as simple cellulitis with oral antibiotics
Severe pain, fever and cirrhosis after seawater exposure suggest Vibrio necrotising infection.
req2: Restrict fluids because of the cirrhosis
He is in septic shock. Resuscitate with balanced crystalloid and add vasopressors.
Withhold cultures to avoid delaying antibiotics
Cultures can be taken quickly and should not delay antibiotics, but they matter.
req3: Flucloxacillin alone
Vibrio vulnificus needs specific cover such as doxycycline with a cephalosporin or carbapenem, plus toxin suppression.
Wait for culture results before antibiotics
Vibrio necrotising fasciitis kills within hours. Treat immediately.
req4: Continue antibiotics and observe the skin markings
Antibiotics cannot penetrate necrotic tissue. Surgical debridement is definitive.
Hyperbaric oxygen before surgery
Hyperbaric oxygen must not delay surgical debridement.
req5: Close the wound primarily after the first debridement
Serial debridement is usually needed. Use negative pressure therapy until clean.
Transfer to the general ward after theatre
He is on vasopressors and needs ICU support.

req1: Wait for thyroid function tests before treating
Thyroid storm is a clinical diagnosis. Treat on the Burch-Wartofsky score.
Give aspirin for the fever
Aspirin displaces thyroid hormone from binding proteins and worsens the storm. Use paracetamol.
req2: Give iodine first to block hormone release
Beta blockade first controls adrenergic effects. Iodine must wait until after a thionamide.
Avoid beta blockers completely because she is pregnant
Propranolol is used in pregnancy for thyroid storm, with caution in cardiac failure.
req3: Iodine before the thionamide
Iodine before a thionamide provides substrate for more hormone synthesis. Thionamide first, iodine an hour later.
Hydrocortisone alone, skip the thionamide
Steroids help block peripheral conversion but do not stop hormone synthesis. A thionamide is essential.
req4: Ignore the urine infection until the storm settles
Infection is the precipitant. Treat it now.
No obstetric involvement until she is stable
At 22 weeks, fetal monitoring and obstetric involvement are part of resuscitation.
req5: Stop all drugs once the heart rate settles
Taper the regimen gradually under endocrinology to avoid relapse.
Radioactive iodine as definitive treatment now
Radioactive iodine is contraindicated in pregnancy.

req1: Give thyroid hormone first, then manage the airway
Hypercapnic respiratory failure kills first. Support ventilation and check glucose.
Sedate with midazolam to settle her
Sedatives are cleared very slowly in myxoedema and worsen respiratory depression.
req2: Levothyroxine before hydrocortisone
Thyroid hormone increases cortisol clearance and can precipitate adrenal crisis. Give hydrocortisone first.
Skip steroids, she has no adrenal disease
Coexisting adrenal insufficiency is possible and dangerous. Give hydrocortisone first.
req3: Oral levothyroxine 50 micrograms daily
Gut absorption is unreliable in myxoedema coma. Use IV loading.
Wait for thyroid results before replacement
Myxoedema coma is clinical and lethal. Treat without delay.
req4: Active rewarming with a forced air blanket at high temperature
Active rewarming causes vasodilation and cardiovascular collapse. Use passive rewarming.
Withhold antibiotics, the fever is absent
Hypothermia masks fever. Treat the pneumonia that likely precipitated the coma.
req5: Correct sodium rapidly with hypertonic saline
Fast correction risks osmotic demyelination. Limit to 8 to 10 mmol/L per 24 hours.
Give sleeping tablets for agitation in ICU
Sedatives are cleared very slowly and can cause relapse. Avoid them.

req1: Wait for the seizure to stop on its own
Status epilepticus causes neuronal damage. Act within the first minute.
Put something in his mouth to stop tongue biting
This causes dental and airway injury. Use a nasopharyngeal airway and suction.
req2: Diazepam 2 mg IV and wait 20 minutes
Underdosing is the commonest failure. Give a full dose and repeat once after 5 minutes.
Go straight to phenytoin without a benzodiazepine
Benzodiazepines are first line. Second line drugs follow two benzodiazepine doses.
req3: A third and fourth benzodiazepine dose
After two doses, more benzodiazepines add respiratory depression without benefit. Give a second line drug.
Oral phenytoin via nasogastric tube
Oral loading is too slow in status epilepticus. Use an IV second line agent.
req4: Keep trying more second line drugs on the ward
Refractory status needs intubation and anaesthetic infusion with EEG monitoring.
Paralyse with rocuronium and stop there
Paralysis hides the seizure but does not stop brain activity. You need anaesthesia and EEG.
req5: Lumbar puncture before the CT
Imaging first to exclude a mass lesion or raised pressure before LP.
Discharge on his old phenytoin dose
Find and treat the cause, and fix why he ran out.

req1: Give the pethidine first, then examine
Red flags must be excluded before any decision. Opioids also blunt the exam.
Refuse to examine him because he is drug seeking
Patients with substance use disorder still get cauda equina and spinal infection. Examine properly.
req2: Give a smaller dose of pethidine as a compromise
Pethidine has toxic metabolites and no role here. Negotiating reinforces the pattern.
Prescribe tramadol to take home
A take-away opioid prescription feeds the pattern and risks harm. Decline clearly.
req3: Strict bed rest for 2 weeks
Bed rest worsens back pain outcomes. Encourage movement.
Prescribe diazepam as a muscle relaxant
Benzodiazepines have little benefit for back pain and add dependence risk with opioids.
req4: Ban him from the department
Bans push risk elsewhere. Refer to addiction and pain services.
Discharge with no referral
He likely has opioid use disorder. Offer agonist therapy and naloxone.

req1: Treat as an electrical burn only and skip trauma imaging
He fell 5 metres after being thrown. Treat as blunt trauma as well.
No cardiac monitoring if the first ECG is normal
High voltage injury needs continuous monitoring for arrhythmia.
req2: Use the Parkland formula from the burn surface area
Surface burns grossly underestimate deep muscle damage in high voltage injury. Titrate to urine output.
Restrict fluids because the burns look small
Deep tissue injury causes rhabdomyolysis. He needs large volume fluid.
req3: Give potassium for the muscle weakness
Muscle breakdown releases potassium. Adding potassium is dangerous.
Treat the potassium only if above 7
ECG changes from hyperkalaemia need immediate calcium regardless of the exact level.
req4: Wait for burns centre transfer before fasciotomy
Compartment syndrome needs immediate decompression.
Fasciotomy without preparing for a potassium surge
Reperfusion releases potassium. Prepare treatment before release.
req5: Discharge once the urine clears
Delayed complications include necrotic muscle, cataract and neuropathy. Transfer to a burns centre.
No eye follow-up needed
High voltage injury causes delayed cataracts. Arrange ophthalmology review.

req1: Observe the airway and intubate if stridor develops
Airway oedema progresses rapidly after inhalation injury. Intubate early before it closes.
Use a small tube to fit the swollen airway
Use the largest tube possible. Small tubes block with soot and limit bronchoscopy.
req2: Trust the pulse oximeter reading of 98%
Pulse oximetry reads carboxyhaemoglobin as oxyhaemoglobin. Use co-oximetry.
Give sodium nitrite for cyanide
Nitrites cause methaemoglobinaemia and worsen oxygen delivery with carbon monoxide. Use hydroxocobalamin.
req3: Include the erythema in the burn area estimate
Erythema is not counted. Including it overestimates fluid needs.
Leave the cooking oil on to protect the burns
Oil traps heat and hides the wounds. Remove it and cool.
req4: Wait for the burns centre to perform escharotomy
Circumferential chest burns restrict ventilation now. Escharotomy is urgent.
No analgesia because the eschar is insensate
Surrounding tissue is painful. Provide analgesia.
req5: Wet dressings during transfer
Wet dressings cause hypothermia. Use cling film and active warming.
Prophylactic IV antibiotics for transfer
Prophylactic antibiotics are not recommended for burns.

req1: Keep him prone and restrained until sedation works
Prone restraint causes positional asphyxia and cardiac arrest. Turn him supine or lateral now.
Sit on his back to stop him moving
Weight on the back restricts breathing. This is a known cause of death.
req2: Haloperidol IV alone and wait 30 minutes
Rapid control is needed. Ketamine IM or midazolam plus droperidol works faster.
Continue physical restraint and avoid drugs
Ongoing struggle drives acidosis and hyperthermia. Rapid chemical sedation is needed.
req3: Send him to psychiatry now that he is calm
Sedation reveals a medical emergency. Check glucose, temperature and gas.
Leave him in a side room to sleep it off
Hyperthermia and acidosis can kill. Monitor fully.
req4: Give paracetamol for the temperature
Hyperthermia here is not a fever. It needs active cooling.
Restrict fluids to avoid pulmonary oedema
He has rhabdomyolysis and acidosis. He needs large volume crystalloid.
req5: Discharge to police custody when awake
Organic causes have not been excluded. Imaging, septic screen and CK monitoring are needed.
Skip the CT, it was clearly drugs
Head injury and infection are possible. Image the brain.

req1: Use the time she was found as the onset time
Onset is the last known well time, which determines thrombolysis eligibility.
Skip glucose, the signs are clearly a stroke
Hypoglycaemia mimics stroke. Check glucose before thrombolysis.
req2: MRI brain before deciding on thrombolysis
Non-contrast CT is faster and sufficient to exclude haemorrhage.
Wait for full blood results before CT
Without a bleeding history, do not delay imaging or thrombolysis for blood results.
req3: Lower the pressure to 140/90 before thrombolysis
Overlowering reduces penumbra perfusion. Target below 185/110.
Sublingual nifedipine for the pressure
This causes unpredictable drops. Use IV labetalol or nicardipine.
req4: Give aspirin 300 mg instead of thrombolysis
She is within the window. Thrombolysis improves outcome. No antiplatelet for 24 hours after.
Wait for neurology review before thrombolysis
Every minute counts. Door to needle should be under 60 minutes.
req5: Wait for the alteplase infusion to finish before referral
Transfer for thrombectomy without waiting for the infusion to finish.
Thrombolysis alone is enough for a large vessel occlusion
Thrombectomy adds major benefit in large vessel occlusion.
req6: Restart the anticoagulant the same day
Early anticoagulation after infarct risks haemorrhagic transformation. Restart at the right interval.
Give her water to test swallowing
She needs a formal swallow assessment before any oral intake.

req1: Lumbar puncture first to confirm the organism
Antibiotics must not be delayed. LP is contraindicated in septicaemic shock.
Wait for blood cultures before antibiotics
Delay increases mortality. Take cultures only if they cost no delay.
req2: Restrict fluids to prevent cerebral oedema
She has septicaemic shock with capillary leak. She needs bolus resuscitation.
Single bolus and no reassessment
Reassess after each bolus to guide further fluid.
req3: Keep giving fluid beyond 80 mL/kg before vasopressors
Persisting with fluid alone causes pulmonary oedema. Start vasoactive support early.
Wait for central access before starting adrenaline
Peripheral or intraosseous infusion is acceptable until central access.
req4: CT brain before treating
Do not delay treatment for imaging. Treat septicaemia now.
Give dexamethasone for meningitis
Dexamethasone is not indicated in meningococcal septicaemia.
req5: Give platelets and plasma to normalise the numbers
Blood products are guided by bleeding and fibrinogen, not numbers alone.
Leave public health notification for the morning team
Contacts need prophylaxis quickly. Notify public health now.

req1: Lift the slab first, then attach monitoring
Release floods the circulation with potassium. Monitor and prepare before release.
Wait for the formal lab potassium
A point of care result or ECG changes are enough to act.
req2: Wait for the lab potassium before treating
Treat ECG changes immediately with calcium.
Give a potassium-sparing diuretic
This would raise potassium further.
req3: Hartmann's solution at high rate
Hartmann's contains potassium. Use normal saline.
Restrict fluids until extrication
Fluids should start before release to prevent kidney injury and arrest.
req4: Routine fasciotomy of both legs
Fasciotomy in necrotic muscle increases infection without benefit. Decide case by case.
Leave the legs and observe for a week
Necrotic muscle drives sepsis and hyperkalaemia. Surgical review now.
req5: Wait for creatinine to rise before dialysis
Hyperkalaemia and myoglobinuria may need early dialysis.
Discharge to the ward once potassium is normal
Potassium can rebound. He needs ICU monitoring.

req1: Go and treat the first critical patient yourself
In a mass casualty incident, someone must command. Declare the incident and take a role.
Keep all current patients in the department
Clear the department to make room for incoming casualties.
req2: Fully resuscitate each patient at the door
Triage at the door does only lifesaving interventions. Full resuscitation blocks the flow.
Triage by arrival order
Use a fixed triage system based on physiology.
req3: Give theatre to the first patient who arrived
Resources go to those with the greatest expected benefit. Allocate explicitly.
Keep the blood for the most injured patient
Allocate blood by survival benefit, and call for regional supply.
req4: Triage once and do not repeat
Patients deteriorate. Retriage every 15 minutes.
Accept every ambulance that arrives
Once capacity is reached, divert to protect patients already here.
req5: Definitive repair of all injuries in the first operation
Damage control surgery saves lives when resources are scarce. Stage definitive care.
Fix all fractures on the first night
Stage orthopaedic fixation. Life threatening injuries take priority.
req6: Send everyone home without a debrief
A structured hot debrief identifies system failures and supports staff.
Debrief only to find who made mistakes
Debriefs focus on systems, not blame.
